a: the prophets
p: The Greek calls the Temple prophets "false prophets" in 26:7, 8, 11 and 16.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.plain: the prophets

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.plain: the false prophets

why: The Hebrew has the plain word "prophets." The Greek translator labels these Temple prophets "false prophets" (pseudoprophetai) here and in 26:7, 11 and 16, and does the same through chapters 26–29 for prophets who oppose Jeremiah. This is more likely the translator's interpretation than a different Hebrew text, since the Hebrew word for "prophet" is the same.
b: No Qumran copy preserves these verses (4QJer-c, 4Q72, begins at 26:10). The addition fits a Greek habit across the book, which also writes "Hananiah the false prophet" (28:1) and "Shemaiah the false prophet" in 29.

a: King Jehoiakim sent men to Egypt: Elnathan son of Achbor, and other men with him, went to Egypt.
p: The Greek lacks Elnathan and his companions.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.orig: וַיִּשְׁלַח הַמֶּלֶךְ יְהוֹיָקִים אֲנָשִׁים מִצְרַיִם אֵת אֶלְנָתָן בֶּן־עַכְבּוֹר וַאֲנָשִׁים אִתּוֹ אֶל־מִצְרָיִם

readings.plain: King Jehoiakim sent men to Egypt: Elnathan son of Achbor, and other men with him, went to Egypt.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.orig: ἐξαπέστειλεν ὁ βασιλεὺς ἄνδρας εἰς Αἴγυπτον
readings.en: the king sent men to Egypt
readings.plain: King Jehoiakim sent men to Egypt.

why: The Hebrew is the longer text and names a man who appears again in 36:12, 25. The Greek's short text may be an abbreviation, or the Hebrew may have added the name from chapter 36. No scroll preserves this verse.

a: Zedekiah son of Josiah
p: The Hebrew says Jehoiakim, but the chapter is about Zedekiah's time; the Greek has no verse 1, and the scroll has only the end of the verse.

readings.w: Inferred from the context of 27:3, 12, 20 and 28:1; no witness read for this part has this reading, and the Plain English Translation follows it
readings.plain: Zedekiah son of Josiah

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.plain: Jehoiakim son of Josiah

why: The Masoretic Text reads Jehoiakim, but the chapter treats Zedekiah as the reigning king (27:3, 12, 20 name Zedekiah and Jeconiah's earlier deportation), and 28:1 dates the same events to Zedekiah's fourth year. A scribal slip is the usual explanation, and the wording of 27:1 is almost the same as 26:1, so a copyist's eye or memory may have gone back to the earlier heading; that is a guess about how the slip happened, not evidence. The Greek has no verse 1 at all, so it supports neither name. The evidence for "Zedekiah" is therefore the chapter's own content, not a manuscript read for this part.
b: The Qumran copy 4QJer-c (4Q72) preserves only the end of the verse ("to Jeremiah from the LORD"), so it cannot decide. The Plain English Translation reads "Zedekiah" because the Hebrew name cannot stand beside 27:3, 12 and 28:1; the Hebrew reading is kept here as the alternative. The notes on 27:1 discuss the further difficulty of the date.

a: All the nations will serve him, and his son, and his son's son, until the time comes for his own land too. Then many nations and great kings will make him their slave.
p: Greek 34 has nothing for 27:7; this is one of its many omissions.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: All the nations will serve him ...
readings.plain: All the nations will serve him, and his son, and his son's son, until the time comes for his own land too. Then many nations and great kings will make him their slave.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (no counterpart)

why: The Hebrew has the verse and nothing in the Greek replaces it. The verse looks forward to Babylon's own fall and may have been added after 539 BC; or the Greek's source lacked it. Without a Qumran copy (no scroll preserves 27:4–12) the choice cannot be settled, so the Plain English Translation keeps the longer Hebrew.
b: The Greek of Jeremiah as a whole is about one-seventh shorter than the Hebrew. The summary on the chapter page lists other small omissions (titles such as "king of Babylon" and "the LORD of Armies").

a: the pillars, the Sea, the stands and the rest of the objects left in this city,
p: The Greek mentions only "the rest of the vessels," not the pillars, Sea and stands.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.orig: עַל־הָעַמֻּדִים וְעַל־הַיָּם וְעַל־הַמְּכֹנוֹת וְעַל יֶתֶר הַכֵּלִים
readings.en: about the pillars, the Sea, the stands and the rest of the objects
readings.plain: the pillars, the Sea, the stands and the rest of the objects left in this city,

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: and the rest of the objects
readings.plain: the rest of the objects

why: The Hebrew names the large bronze pieces of the Temple. The Greek has a much shorter form of 27:19–22. The long text may be an expansion based on 2 Kings 25:13–17 and 52:17–23, or the Greek may have abbreviated. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew; this variant goes together with the one at 27:22.

a: 'They will be taken to Babylon, and there they will stay until the day I call for them, the LORD declares. Then I will bring them up and return them to this place.'
t: A promise of return, or only of exile?
p: The Greek says the vessels will go to Babylon and says nothing of their return.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.orig: בָּבֶלָה יוּבָאוּ וְשָׁמָּה יִהְיוּ עַד יוֹם פָּקְדִי אֹתָם ... וְהַעֲלִיתִים וַהֲשִׁיבֹתִים אֶל־הַמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה
readings.en: to Babylon they will be brought, and there they will be until the day I visit them ... then I will bring them up and bring them back to this place
readings.plain: 'They will be taken to Babylon, and there they will stay until the day I call for them, the LORD declares. Then I will bring them up and return them to this place.'

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: into Babylon they will enter, says the Lord
readings.plain: 'They will be taken to Babylon, the LORD declares.'

why: The Hebrew promises both exile and return. The Greek keeps only the threat, so Jeremiah's answer to Hananiah would be wholly negative. The promise of return may have been added by a later editor who knew that Cyrus returned the vessels (Ezra 1:7–11), or the Greek translator's source may have lacked it. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew and notes that the promise points to a time "I call for them," not Hananiah's two years.
b: Goes with the variant at 27:19. No scroll preserves 27:16–22.

a: It was in that same year, early in the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fourth year, in the fifth month
t: "That same year, early in the reign"
p: The Greek reads only "in the fourth year of Zedekiah, in the fifth month."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.orig: וַיְהִי בַּשָּׁנָה הַהִיא בְּרֵאשִׁית מַמְלֶכֶת צִדְקִיָּה ... בַּשָּׁנָה הָרְבִעִית בַּחֹדֶשׁ הַחֲמִישִׁי
readings.en: In that year, at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah ... in the fourth year, in the fifth month
readings.plain: It was in that same year, early in the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fourth year, in the fifth month

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.orig: ἐν τῷ τετάρτῳ ἔτει Σεδεκία βασιλέως Ἰούδα ἐν μηνὶ τῷ πέμπτῳ
readings.en: in the fourth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fifth month
readings.plain: It was in the fourth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fifth month

why: The Hebrew places the event "in that year" (the year of chapter 27) and "at the beginning of the reign," then says "in the fourth year," which is a tension. The Greek has only the date. The Hebrew phrase may have been added to link chapters 27 and 28, perhaps when 27:1 was changed (see there). The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew and notes the tension.
b: No scroll preserves chapter 28. The Greek also calls Hananiah "the false prophet."

a: war, disaster and disease
t: War only, or war, disaster and disease?
p: The Greek has only "war."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: for war, for disaster and for disease
readings.plain: war, disaster and disease

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 35:8)
readings.plain: war

why: The Greek has no counterpart to "disaster" and "disease." This bears on the test of a prophet (28:8-9): in the Hebrew the earlier prophets announced a three-part judgment, in the Greek only war. Either the Hebrew was expanded or a translator dropped part of a stock list. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew; no scroll preserves chapter 28.

a: but you will make yoke-bars of iron in their place
p: The Greek makes the LORD the one who forges the iron yoke.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and you will make in their place bars of iron
readings.plain: but you will make yoke-bars of iron in their place

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.orig: καὶ ποιήσω ἀντ᾽ αὐτῶν κλοιοὺς σιδηροῦς
readings.en: and I will make in their place collars of iron
readings.plain: but I will make yoke-bars of iron in their place

why: The Hebrew word, as pointed, has Hananiah as the one who makes the iron bars: his false hope will result in a heavier yoke through the people's own revolt. The Greek makes God the maker, which fits 28:14 ("I have put a yoke of iron"). The Hebrew is the harder reading and fits Jeremiah's habit of blaming people's own choices, so the Plain English Translation follows it. Without a scroll the question is open.
b: No scroll preserves chapter 28. The difference is only one vowel on the unpointed consonants, so the Greek may reflect a different reading of the same letters.

a: of the city I sent you to as exiles
p: The Greek says "land."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.plain: of the city I sent you to as exiles

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.plain: of the land I sent you to as exiles

why: The Hebrew says "city" and the context (Babylon) fits it. The Greek "land" may be a different reading of the Hebrew word or an easing of it. No scroll preserves this verse.
b: The Greek also reads "pray for them" where the Hebrew says "pray for it."

a: I mean to give you a future, and hope with it
t: "A future and a hope" in Hebrew and Greek
p: The Greek says only "to give you these things."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: to give you an outcome (a future) and a hope
readings.plain: I mean to give you a future, and hope with it

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.plain: to give you these things

why: The Hebrew acharit vetiqvah is the source of the famous English line about a future and a hope. The Greek lacks the second noun and has a plain "to give you these things." The Hebrew may have been expanded, or the Greek abridged. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew; Jeremiah 31:17 has the same pair of words. No scroll preserves this verse.

a: I will let you find me, the LORD declares. I will turn your fortunes around. I will gather you from all the nations and all the places where I have driven you, the LORD declares, and I will bring you back to the place I sent you away from into exile.
p: The Greek has only "I will appear to you."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.orig: וְנִמְצֵאתִי לָכֶם ... וְהֵשִׁבֹתִי אֶתְכֶם אֶל־הַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר־הִגְלֵיתִי אֶתְכֶם מִשָּׁם
readings.en: I will let myself be found ... and I will bring you back to the place from which I exiled you
readings.plain: I will let you find me, the LORD declares. I will turn your fortunes around. I will gather you from all the nations and all the places where I have driven you, the LORD declares, and I will bring you back to the place I sent you away from into exile.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: and I will appear to you
readings.plain: I will appear to you.

why: The Hebrew has a long promise of return from all nations, which goes beyond the seventy years of verse 10 and speaks of a gathering from "all the nations." The Greek has a short line. Scholars who favor the shorter text think the Hebrew adds a wider gathering after the dispersion grew; others think the Greek abridged. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

a: But the LORD says this about the king who sits on David's throne, and about all the people living in this city, your relatives who did not go out with you into exile:
p: Verses 16–20 go together: the Greek has nothing for them.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.plain: But the LORD says this about the king who sits on David's throne, and about all the people living in this city, your relatives who did not go out with you into exile:

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (no counterpart)

why: The Greek runs from 29:15 straight to 29:21. The five verses add a judgment on the king and the people left in Jerusalem, which the letter's other parts do not need, and which may be a later expansion; or a copyist's eye may have jumped from one "the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says this" to another. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew. No scroll preserves these verses.

p: Goes with 29:16: the Greek has nothing for this verse.

p: Goes with 29:16: the Greek has nothing for this verse.

readings.plain: So you, all the exiles I sent away from Jerusalem to Babylon, hear the word of the LORD.

a: You are the one who sent letters in your own name
p: The Greek has the LORD say, "I did not send you in my name."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: you sent letters in your own name
readings.plain: You are the one who sent letters in your own name

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 36:25)
readings.orig: Οὐκ ἀπέστειλά σε τῷ ὀνόματί μου
readings.en: I did not send you in my name
readings.plain: I did not send you in my name

why: The Hebrew charges Shemaiah with writing letters on his own authority to Jerusalem (to Zephaniah and the priests). The Greek puts the charge in a different mouth: the LORD says he did not send Shemaiah, and it has no mention of the letters at this point. The Hebrew fits the next verses, which quote the letter (29:26-28), and 29:31 makes the same point about sending. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew; no scroll preserves the verse.

a: As for you, Jacob my servant, do not be afraid, the LORD declares;
t: Verses 10–11 are elsewhere in the Greek
p: The Greek has no 30:10–11 here, but it has the same words at its chapter 26:27–28 (Hebrew 46:27–28).

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: And you, do not fear, my servant Jacob, declares the LORD
readings.plain: As for you, Jacob my servant, do not be afraid, the LORD declares;

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (omitted here; present at Greek 26:27–28)

why: The Greek omits 30:10–11 in this place because it has the same lines in the oracle against Egypt (Hebrew 46:27–28, Greek 26:27–28). The Hebrew has the passage twice. The question is whether it first belonged to Egypt's oracle, to the Book of Consolation, or to both. The poem fits both places. The Plain English Translation keeps both. Goes with 30:11; no scroll preserves 30:10–11.
b: The anchor shows only the first line because the Plain English Translation sets this verse as poetry; the whole of verses 10 and 11 is missing in the Greek.

a: For I am with you, to save you, the LORD declares.
t: Verses 10–11 are elsewhere in the Greek (continued)
p: Goes with 30:10: the whole verse is missing in the Greek at this place.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: For I am with you, declares the LORD, to save you
readings.plain: For I am with you, to save you, the LORD declares.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (omitted here; present at Greek 26:28)

why: See the variant at 30:10. The whole of verse 11 is absent from the Greek of chapter 30.

a: Why cry out about your fracture?
t: A repeated verse the Greek lacks
p: The Greek omits 30:15, which repeats the words of 30:14.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: Why do you cry out over your fracture?
readings.plain: Why cry out about your fracture?

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (no counterpart)

why: The verse repeats the last lines of 30:14 and adds a cry of complaint. The Greek has nothing here. The omission may come from a scribe's eye skipping from one "because of how great your guilt" to the next, or the Hebrew may have added the repetition. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew; the anchor is the first line only, since the Plain English Translation sets the verse as poetry. No scroll preserves 30:15.

a: And you will be my people
p: The Greek lacks 30:22; the Qumran copy 4QJer-c has it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4QJer-c (4Q72), which preserves "and you will be to me a people and I will be to you..."
readings.en: And you will be a people to me
readings.plain: And you will be my people

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (no counterpart)

why: The Qumran copy 4Q72 preserves most of the verse (its last word is restored), so the verse was in the Hebrew of one text type in the first century BC. The Greek lacks it in this place, but has the same formula in 31:1 and 31:33. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew with the scroll. The anchor shows only the first line, since the verse is poetry.
b: The scroll 4QJer-c, as read in the transcription of Abegg, Bowley and Cook, agrees with the Masoretic Text in what it preserves of chapters 30–31 apart from spelling and these readings: 30:17 has nidachat and only the second half of the verse, from "because they called you an outcast"; 30:18 reads "and it will be rebuilt" (venivneh); 31:8 reads "and I will gather them"; 31:9 and 31:12 read al where the Masoretic Text has el; and 31:22 has a stray letter. The first half of 30:17 is not preserved.

a: found favor in the wilderness
p: The Greek reads quite differently: "I found warmth in the wilderness."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4QJer-c (4Q72), which preserves "found favor in the wilderness"
readings.plain: found favor in the wilderness

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: I found heat/warmth in the wilderness
readings.plain: I found warmth in the wilderness

why: The scroll agrees with the Hebrew. The Greek seems to read chen (favor) as cham (warm) and to take the verb as "I found," and then treats the end of the line as a command, "Go, and do not destroy Israel." This is probably a different reading of the same letters and not a different text.
b: The line goes with the second half of the verse, which the Greek renders differently.

a: the LORD appeared to me
p: The Greek says the LORD appeared "to him."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4QJer-c (4Q72) preserves "appeared to me"
readings.plain: the LORD appeared to me

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.plain: the LORD appeared to him

why: The Hebrew has the first person, with an unexplained speaker: Israel, or the prophet speaking for Israel. The scroll has the same. The Greek smooths it to the third person, making the line part of the narration. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew and the scroll.

a: LORD, save your people
p: The Hebrew vocalization reads a prayer; the Greek reads a statement.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex) (vocalized as an imperative); 4QJer-c (4Q72) spells the verb with a yod, which fits either
readings.plain: LORD, save your people

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: The Lord has saved his people
readings.plain: The LORD has saved his people

why: The Masoretic pointing makes the line a prayer, which fits the shout of the crowd. The Greek reads the verb as a perfect, "has saved," a cry of thanks, as the people see the rescue as done. The scroll spells it hwsy', the full spelling of either form. The Plain English Translation follows the pointed Hebrew; both fit the poem.

a: Among them are the blind and the lame
t: The blind and the lame, or the Passover?
p: The Greek has "at the feast of the Passover" where the Hebrew has "the blind and the lame."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4QJer-c (4Q72) preserves the consonants of "and lame" (wpsh)
readings.plain: Among them are the blind and the lame

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: at the feast of the Passover
readings.plain: At the feast of the Passover

why: The Hebrew consonants psch can be read as pisseach (lame) or pesach (Passover). The Greek seems to have taken the second, and left out the blind, giving a returning crowd that comes home at Passover. The Hebrew and the scroll's consonants permit either, but "blind and lame" fits the list that follows (the pregnant woman and the one in labor) and the pairs in Isaiah 35:5–6. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

a: I will gather them
t: "I will gather them": form of the verb
p: The scroll has a first-person form where the Masoretic Text has a perfect with "and."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.plain: I will gather them

readings.w: 4QJer-c (4Q72), a visible reading
readings.plain: I will gather them

why: The two forms differ in how the verb is built (the Masoretic perfect with waw, the scroll an imperfect with "and"); both mean "I will gather them," so the Plain English Translation reads the same for both.

a: with prayers for mercy
p: The Greek has "in comfort."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.plain: with prayers for mercy

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.plain: with comfort

why: The Hebrew tachanunim ("pleas for favor") and the Greek "comfort" (which would be tanchumim in Hebrew) differ by a few letters. The Greek makes the line positive: weeping on the way out, comfort on the way home. The Hebrew is the harder reading, since the returning people still plead. 4QJer-c is damaged here: the word for "prayers for mercy" is restored in brackets, so the scroll gives no reading. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

a: to streams of water
p: The scroll and the Greek have al and epi where the Masoretic Text has el.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.plain: to streams of water

readings.w: 4QJer-c (4Q72), where al is a visible reading; Greek (Septuagint), Swete's Vaticanus (Greek 38:9), epi ("upon, beside")
readings.orig: עַל נַחֲלֵי מָיִם / ἐπὶ διώρυγας ὑδάτων
readings.plain: to streams of water

why: Two witnesses, the scroll and the Greek, agree on al, which can mean "by, along" (compare Psalm 23:2) as well as "to." In late Hebrew al and el are often interchanged, so the sense hardly changes. The Plain English Translation keeps "to," which suits both. The agreement of two independent witnesses against the Masoretic Text is still worth recording.

a: they will stream to the LORD's good gifts
p: The scroll and the Greek have al and epi where the Masoretic Text has el.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and they will stream to the goodness of the LORD
readings.plain: they will stream to the LORD's good gifts

readings.w: 4QJer-c (4Q72), where al is a visible reading; Greek (Septuagint), Swete's Vaticanus (Greek 38:12), ep' agatha
readings.orig: וְנָהֲרוּ עַל טוּב יְהוָה / ἐπ᾽ ἀγαθὰ Κυρίου
readings.en: and they will stream (or shine) over the goodness of the LORD
readings.plain: they will stream to the LORD's good gifts

why: Again the scroll and the Greek agree against the Masoretic Text. The preposition al matches the three al phrases that follow (over the grain, the new wine, the oil) and so may be the original. It does not decide the question of the note, whether nahar is "stream" or "shine"; either verb can take al or el. The Plain English Translation keeps the stream picture and an English "to," as the three following phrases also have.

a: after my turning
p: The Greek reads "after my captivity."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.plain: after my turning

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.plain: after my captivity

why: The Hebrew shuvi ("my turning") can mean turning back or turning away. The Greek aichmalosia translates shevuti ("my captivity"), the same letters except one. The Hebrew is the Jeremiah pun on shuv (the key word of the book); the Greek may have read it the other way. The Qumran copy 4QJer-c is broken at this word.

a: For the LORD has created a new thing in the land
t: The woman who surrounds a man, or a new planting?
p: The Greek says "the LORD has created salvation for a new planting" and lacks the saying about the woman.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.orig: כִּי־בָרָא יְהוָה חֲדָשָׁה בָּאָרֶץ נְקֵבָה תְסוֹבֵב גָּבֶר
readings.en: For the LORD has created a new thing in the land: a female will surround a man
readings.plain: For the LORD has created a new thing in the land

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.orig: ὅτι ἔκτισεν Κύριος σωτηρίαν εἰς καταφύτευσιν καινήν
readings.en: For the Lord has created salvation for a new planting
readings.plain: For the LORD has created salvation for a new planting

why: The Greek's "a new planting" suggests a different reading of the Hebrew, and its next words are "in salvation men will go about," which has no woman in it. The Hebrew line is a famous puzzle (see the note on the next line). Whether the Greek is the original and the Hebrew a corruption, or the reverse, is much debated. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew, which both Jewish and early Christian readers knew. The Qumran copy has only part of the verse: the words for "female" and "surround" are restored in brackets.
b: Goes with the note on the next line, "a woman will surround a man."

a: though I had married them
p: The Greek, and Hebrews 8:9 after it, have "I did not care for them."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and I was a husband (master) to them
readings.plain: though I had married them

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus; quoted in Hebrews 8:9 (Greek: ἠμέλησα)
readings.plain: though I neglected them

why: Ba'al as a verb means to be a husband or master (compare 3:14). The Greek ameleo ("neglect, disregard") probably reflects a different sense of the Hebrew verb, "reject" or "disregard" in place of "be a husband to." Hebrews 8:9 quotes the Greek form. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew, in which the broken covenant is one made like a marriage; no scroll preserves 31:32–34.
b: Hebrews uses Jeremiah in its Greek form in 8:8–12. Where Hebrews differs from the Hebrew, the difference comes from the Greek of Jeremiah.

a: I will put my law inside them
p: The Greek has "I will give my laws into their mind."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: I will put my law within them
readings.plain: I will put my law inside them

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus; quoted in Hebrews 8:10 and 10:16
readings.orig: διδοὺς δώσω νόμους μου εἰς τὴν διάνοιαν αὐτῶν
readings.en: giving I will give my laws into their mind
readings.plain: I will put my laws into their minds

why: The Hebrew has a singular "law" and "inside them" (their inner being). The Greek has the plural "laws" and "mind." Hebrews 8:10 and 10:16 use the Greek form. Both forms are meaningful, but only the Hebrew is the Masoretic and the Plain English Translation follows it. No scroll preserves 31:33.

a: one person his neighbor
p: The Greek, and Hebrews 8:11 after it, have "fellow citizen."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.plain: one person his neighbor

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 38:34); quoted in Hebrews 8:11 in the text most editors print (some manuscripts there have "neighbor")
readings.plain: one person his fellow citizen

why: The Greek translator rendered re'ehu ("his neighbor, companion") as "his fellow citizen." Hebrews 8:11 quotes the passage in its Greek form, as it does at 31:32, so the New Testament form of the promise is shaped by the Greek, not directly by the Hebrew. The difference is small in sense: both mean the person next to you. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew; no scroll preserves 31:32-34.
b: Where the Greek of Jeremiah and Hebrews agree against the Hebrew, as here and at 31:32, the quotation reflects the Greek translation Hebrews' readers used.
